title: Trust and Safety as a Platform
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (paragraph for paragraph, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, acceptance criteria AC-1 to AC-3, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the trust-and-safety-architecture entry in journal-spec.json. Added units not in the published text: the roadmap paragraph p03 and the synthesis paragraph p59.

know: The five functions of trust and safety (policy, detection, decision, enforcement, review and redress) plus measurement, the speed at which each changes and how each fails; policies as versioned reference data.

The moderation pipeline: synchronous gate and asynchronous path, risk-tiered moderation modes, human review queues and the random sample, LLMs for the grey zone; the enforcement ladder and its propagation to every consumer; notice and action, case management, appeals and statements of reasons as a by-product.
The trust-and-safety metrics (prevalence, time to action, precision, recall, overturn rate, report rate, reviewer agreement) and how each misleads.
believe: A removal is not finished when the listing's status changes; it is finished when the last consumer has acknowledged it.
Trust and safety pays to share across brands from the first year, but only the machinery, evidence and lawful signals; policy judgement stays local.
can_do: Draw the trust-and-safety components and their interfaces, with one decision service as the only writer of decision records.
Defend a risk-tiered moderation design instead of a choice between pre- and post-moderation, and say what must happen in every system when a listing or account is restricted.
Decide which trust-and-safety components a group shares and which each brand keeps.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an incomplete removal and an undeclared demotion practice, the reader names what is missing and what the design does.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A fraudulent listing removed at 09:00 still appears in a 10:00 alert digest and in a similar-items carousel, its seller's open payout goes out, and the ranking team has been quietly demoting suspected scams for months. Using only this chapter: what is missing, and what does the design do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Enforcement is an EnforcementApplied event from the decision service that every consumer applies idempotently and acknowledges: alerts drop queued notifications and exclude the listing from digests, recommendations evict it, payments hold or freeze per policy; a propagation monitor tracks time to the last acknowledgement, and the removal is not done until then. Demotion is a restriction under Article 17 of the DSA, so it must go through the decision service with a decision record and a statement of reasons.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The four-stacks history and the question 'what did we remove, why, and did it disappear'; the Veldmark phishing incident and the group's four stacks; the five functions and policies as data; the moderation pipeline with the public practice behind it, modes, human review and LLMs; enforcement and its propagation; intake, cases, appeals and statements of reasons; metrics; what a group shares and how verticals differ; trade-offs, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: the DSA, public engineering sources (Meta's Sigma, Stripe Radar, OLX), the Which? 2024 test, the 2015 leboncoin ruling and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.
Given a proposal to choose between pre- and post-moderation for the whole marketplace, the reader replaces it with risk tiers and names the two public cases that show why.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your product director wants one rule for the whole marketplace: either every listing is checked before it goes live, or everything goes live at once and is checked afterwards. Using only this chapter: what do you propose instead, and which public cases support it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Neither: set the moderation mode per risk tier from the category's risk, the seller's trust level and the listing's risk score, with a synchronous gate for every action and slower checks on an asynchronous path (a cheap book goes live on the gate, a new account's first rental waits for image and duplicate checks), and time budgets per tier agreed with the general managers. Treat every material edit as a new submission, because in the Which? 2024 test edited scam ads passed review in minutes; and describe the mode truthfully, because in 2015 a Paris court found leboncoin guilty of misleading practices for claiming all ads were validated.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposal to centralize moderators under one group policy and report removals to the board, the reader says what the group shares, what stays with each brand, who decides on cross-brand signals and what to report instead.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A group of four marketplace brands proposes to merge all moderators into one central team with one policy, and to report the number of listings removed to the board each month. Using only this chapter: what would you share, what would you keep per brand, who decides which signals cross brands, and what would you report instead?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Share the machinery: decision service and decision record, enforcement events and propagation monitor, case tooling, evidence store, statement-of-reasons service, rule runtime and lifecycle, the policy registry with local content, base models; share hashed block lists only where the Data Protection Officer approves them (purpose, retention, impact assessment), never raw message content. Keep per brand: policy overlays, thresholds and risk appetite, reviewers with language skills, vertical detectors. Report sampled prevalence of fraudulent listings by brand with its trend, next to time to action on fraud reports, not removal counts.

audience.who: Chief architects of marketplace groups, heads of trust and safety and their engineering leads, and principal engineers who own insertion, search, messaging, alerts or ranking and need to know where those systems meet moderation.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a rules engine, an ML classifier and an LLM are.

From earlier chapters: Veldmark (fictional) and its brands Tradeyard, Motorvane, Hearthly and Keybridge, the cast (Ingrid Halvorsen, Aisha Rahman, Lucía Ortega), the Common Ground program and the architecture advice forum, Yardstick, Tradeyard Safe Deal, the Rotterdam city bike, bounded contexts, the listing lifecycle with its enforcement overlay, the publication pipeline, the event backbone, Part IV's search, recommendations and alerts, and the failure patterns Ghost Inventory, Moderation as an Afterthought and Set-and-Forget AI.
From the part introduction: trust as a platform capability and Veldmark's four trust-and-safety stacks.
does_not_know: Trust-and-safety vocabulary: policy (as a versioned record), moderation pipeline, enforcement action, case, pre- and post-moderation, prevalence, overturn rate, trusted flagger.
The DSA articles on notice and action (16), statements of reasons (17), internal complaints (20), out-of-court settlement (21), trusted flaggers (22) and the Transparency Database (24(5)).

thesis.question: How should trust and safety be architected across listings, users, messages and transactions?
thesis.claim: Trust and safety should be built as five separately owned functions (policy, detection, decision, enforcement, review and redress) plus measurement, joined by one decision record that a single decision service writes: policies are versioned reference data that every rule, model, reviewer guideline and notice cites; the moderation mode is set per risk tier of category, seller and listing rather than chosen once; an enforcement action, demotion included, is done only when every consumer (search, alerts, recommendations, messaging, SEO pages, ads, payments, partner feeds) has acknowledged its EnforcementApplied event; the platform is judged on sampled prevalence, time to action, precision and appeal overturn rate rather than removal counts; and a group shares this machinery and lawful hashed block lists while each brand keeps its policy overlays, thresholds, reviewers and vertical detectors.
thesis.disputed_by: The common view that trust and safety is an operations function: a review queue attached to insertion, staffed per brand or outsourced, measured by items reviewed and listings removed, with a removal finished once the listing's status changes, and with sharing across a group meaning centralized moderators and one policy.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this makes the decision record schema and the single-writer rule a group decision, sets propagation targets per consumer and watches p95 and worst case, lets the Data Protection Officer decide which signals cross brands, leaves risk tiers and thresholds to marketplace general managers within group guardrails, and puts sampled prevalence of fraudulent listings by brand, next to time to action on fraud reports, in front of the board.
thesis.how_why: On 7 March 2027 Tradeyard NL suspended a phishing account seven minutes after Femke's report, yet its phone number also had a Motorvane account no one could see, Tradeyard Belgium received the new rule on Wednesday, Poland and Portugal never did, and the sellers it had already contacted got no warning: four stacks with 210 moderators, three appeal processes and five ways of producing statements of reasons could not share a signal. A blind sample of 4,000 Tradeyard NL listings a week found about 0.6% violating policy against the 0.2% removal counts suggested. The shared platform, live for Tradeyard NL and BE in November 2027, targets 96% automation from 94%, a median time to action on fraud reports under 30 minutes from 3 hours 10 minutes, and an alert when the overturn rate of a policy exceeds 10%.

supporting_claims.claim: Trust and safety is five functions (policy, detection, decision, enforcement, review and redress) plus measurement, built as separate components joined by one decision record that only the decision service writes, with policies as versioned reference data that every rule, model, guideline and notice cites.

The moderation mode is set per risk tier of category, seller and listing, using a synchronous gate and an asynchronous path, human queues designed for the grey zone, labels and legal duties, and LLMs only in the grey zone, rather than chosen once between pre- and post-moderation.

An enforcement action, demotion included, is a rung on a ladder chosen by the decision service and is done only when every consumer holding a copy has applied and acknowledged its EnforcementApplied event.
Notices, cases, appeals and statements of reasons are entities linked to decision records, so redress and regulatory output are views of the record rather than separate projects.

The platform is judged on sampled prevalence, time to action to the last acknowledgement, precision and appeal overturn rate, computed from decision records and samples per policy and detector, not on removal counts or queue sizes.
A group shares the machinery, the evidence and the hashed signals its Data Protection Officer approves, while each brand keeps its policy overlays, thresholds, reviewers and vertical detectors.

role.contribution: Builds the platform the rest of the part plugs into, the decision service, decision record, enforcement propagation, appeals and metrics, and sets out which of it a group shares.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene poses the problem (four stacks that cannot share a signal and Ingrid's question which parts are one platform); sharing answers it after the body has built the parts
architecture, enforcement, intake and measuring follow one decision through its life: detected and decided, enforced everywhere, contested and reported, then counted

flow.rationale: The scene ends on Ingrid's question, which parts of trust and safety are one platform and which stay four, and the body supplies, in order, what that answer needs. The five functions and policies as data come first because every later component is named by the function it serves and cites a policy version. The pipeline then shows how detection and decision work, opening with the public evidence (Sigma, Stripe Radar, OLX, Adevinta's shared OCR service) that the reference design, labeled as an inference, is assembled from; enforcement follows because it acts on what the decision service decided; intake, cases and appeals come next because an appeal reverses an enforced decision and a statement of reasons describes one; measurement comes after them because its figures are computed from decision records, samples and overturns. The sharing decision comes after measurement because it can only be argued once every shared component has been introduced; vertical differences follow it directly because they justify its local side (thresholds, policy overlays, vertical detectors). Trade-offs, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions apply the whole design, so they come last.

hook.content: A keyword filter after the first spam wave, a review queue after the first press story, a report button after the first regulator letter: ten years later a group has four moderation stacks that cannot share a signal, and nobody can answer what did we remove last month, why, and did it actually disappear?

bridge.from_reader_world: Architects who built Part IV's search, recommendations and alerts to put a listing in front of buyers within seconds.
bridge.to_topic: Each of those surfaces must also obey a removal, so trust and safety has to be architected as a platform that reaches all of them, not a queue beside insertion.

thesis_statement.text: Treat trust and safety as a platform capability: five functions built as separate components joined by one decision record, enforcement done only when every system holding a copy has applied it, metrics of harm rather than activity, and shared machinery with local policy.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Four Stacks and One Phishing Link

sections.heading: Concepts: The Five Functions of Trust and Safety
sections.controlling_idea: Trust and safety splits into five functions plus measurement, defined by what each decides, how fast it changes and how it fails, and policies are the versioned reference data every function cites.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the functions and the policy record the architecture is built from.

flow.rationale: The functions are named first, then the working terms, then the first function's record in detail; the policy record names detectors and actions only by the function they serve, which is all the reader has at this point, and sections 3 and 4 develop them. Placed after the pipeline, the policy record would arrive after components that already cite it.

transition_in.carries_over: Ingrid's question which parts are one platform.
transition_in.introduces: Splitting trust and safety into functions, the prerequisite for answering it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Trust and safety is easier to architect once it is split into five functions (policy, detection, decision, enforcement, review and redress) that change at different speeds and fail in different ways.

evidence.what: Function table: question, speed of change, typical failure.
evidence.shows: Each function has its own pace and failure, so each needs its own component and owner.

evidence.what: Figure 1: five gears joined by one record ribbon.
evidence.shows: The functions are joined by one decision record and watched by measurement.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Measurement and transparency is a sixth concern that runs across all five functions.

transition_in.introduces: The concern that spans them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five working terms are used throughout the chapter: policy, moderation pipeline, enforcement action, case and T&S metrics, three of which the chapter owns.

evidence.what: 'No live animals in Tradeyard PT except through registered breeders' is a policy, a keyword list is not; a ring of 26 accounts is one case, not 180 tickets.
evidence.shows: The examples separate each term from what it is often confused with.

transition_in.introduces: The terms the rest of the chapter uses for their parts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The functions decide on actors as well as listings, and the decision record links the two views; a takeover account with clean listings and a verified badge is the sharpest actor case; Trust is its own bounded context in which a listing is a subject under evaluation.

evidence.what: A weapon or a discriminatory rental ad violates on its own; a fraud ring or a takeover account is a problem even when every listing looks clean.
evidence.shows: Shows why decisions must cover both views.

evidence.what: A takeover account whose listings look clean while its verified badge still vouches for it to buyers.
evidence.shows: Introduces the badge that failure mode 10 recaps.

transition_in.introduces: Decisions about actors.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The most underrated design decision is to treat policies as data: a registry of versioned policy records that rules, models, reviewer guidelines, notices and reports all point to.

evidence.what: Veldmark's POL-FRAUD-PAYLINK v3 record: scope, statement, ground, DSA category, detectors, allowed actions, guideline, user-facing reason, owner.
evidence.shows: A policy record is concrete enough to cite, localize and review.

transition_in.carries_over: The five functions and their terms.
transition_in.introduces: The first function, policy, built as data.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Policies as data let a decision cite policy ID and version, let countries add overlays without forking the platform, and move legal review into the registry.

transition_in.introduces: Three consequences of keeping policies as data.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: As with category trees, a decision must stay explainable under the policy version in force when it was taken.

evidence.what: categories-and-taxonomies treats category trees as versioned reference data.
evidence.shows: The same versioning reasoning applies, with the added duty of explaining past decisions.

sections.heading: Architecture: The Moderation Pipeline and Its Components
sections.controlling_idea: The moderation pipeline, anchored first in what the public record documents, is a set of components around one decision service, run at two speeds whose split, together with the moderation mode, human queues and LLM use, is set by risk.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the components and sets the moderation mode by risk tier.

additional_patterns.applies_to: p18 to p20: the gate a listing meets first, then the asynchronous path after it

flow.rationale: The public evidence first, because the reference design is assembled from it and labeled as an inference; then the whole component set; then the two speeds a listing meets, the risk decision that splits them and the range of modes it produces; then human review, sampling and LLMs, which act on what the automated path leaves uncertain. Placed before the components, the modes would describe paths the reader cannot locate. The evidence was tried at the end of the section (round 3 readers read it as an appendix) and directly after the component table (round 5 readers found it interrupted the component walkthrough and repeated the section's opening), so it now opens the section and the reference-design paragraph points back to it instead of listing the sources a second time.

transition_in.introduces: The components that implement them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Classifieds companies publish little about trust and safety, but what they publish shows shared moderation in a portfolio, shared models, real-time chat moderation, rules deployed in minutes and rule operations, enough to anchor the design but not to describe any company.

evidence.what: Adevinta Annual Report 2023 (April 2024): chat and moderation among the first consolidated capabilities.
evidence.shows: A multi-country group shared moderation early.

evidence.what: Adevinta Tech Blog (March 2023): central Text in Image OCR service, 100 million to 330 million requests a month.
evidence.shows: A shared detector with many tenants.

evidence.what: OLX Group (January 2026): real-time chat moderation and image blocking.
evidence.shows: Chat moderation in production.

evidence.what: Engineering at Meta (2015): Sigma, rules hot-swapped at over a million requests a second.
evidence.shows: A rule should reach production in minutes, which Tradeyard Belgium lacked when the rule took until Wednesday.

evidence.what: Stripe Radar documentation (n.d.): backtesting, shadow mode, rollout, audit.
evidence.shows: Rule lifecycle transfers to moderation.

evidence.what: INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED callout on Adevinta-group job postings (2025–2026).
evidence.shows: Labels the shared-platform reading as inference.

advances_thesis.how: Grounds the shared-platform design in dated public sources and labels the inference.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The reference architecture, assembled from public building blocks and labeled as an inference, makes one decision service the only writer of decision records, with every other component feeding it or deriving from its records.

evidence.what: Meta's Sigma (2015), Stripe Radar's rule operations, OLX's chat moderation, the DSA, the Ofcom-commissioned report (July 2026).
evidence.shows: The design is assembled from public evidence, not a description of any company.

evidence.what: Figure 2: detection and review feed one decision service.
evidence.shows: All outputs derive from decision records.

evidence.what: Component table: responsibility and key interface of eleven components.
evidence.shows: Each function has a component with a defined interface.

transition_in.carries_over: The public building blocks just surveyed.
transition_in.introduces: The reference architecture assembled from them and its single decision writer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The synchronous gate sits inside the user's action with a budget of a few hundred milliseconds, so it can afford only rules, block-list lookups and a cheap model, and answers allow, hold or reject.

transition_in.introduces: The first component a listing meets, the gate.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The asynchronous path runs slower detectors on events after the action and can still demote, hold or remove a listing that is already live.

transition_in.introduces: The slower checks after the action.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Which checks run in which path is a risk decision, not a technical one: a cheap book can go live on the gate, while a rental in a fake-rental city should wait for image and duplicate checks.

evidence.what: A €15 children's book versus a rental flat in a city with a fake-rental problem.
evidence.shows: The harm of exposure, not the technology, decides the path.

evidence.what: Figure 3: two lanes, the book goes live, the rental waits.
evidence.shows: The same split drawn as a road.

transition_in.introduces: What decides which check runs where.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Pre-moderation and post-moderation are the ends of a spectrum, and large platforms run several points on it at once.

evidence.what: Four modes compared on time to live, exposure, cost and fit.
evidence.shows: Each mode trades exposure against cost and speed.

transition_in.introduces: The full range of moderation modes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The design that works is risk-tiered: the mode depends on the category's risk, the seller's trust level and the listing's risk score.

evidence.what: A verified dealer's car from a DMS feed goes live on the gate; a new account's first rental waits for the full check.
evidence.shows: Shows two tiers side by side.

transition_in.introduces: Choosing the mode per risk tier.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two public cases show why the mode matters: edits must be re-moderated as new submissions, and the terms must describe the mode the platform actually runs.

evidence.what: Which? December 2024 test: edited scam ads passed review in minutes; one Facebook ad live almost 48 hours.
evidence.shows: Re-scoring only at creation lets edited scams through.

evidence.what: December 2015 Paris ruling against leboncoin for claiming all ads were validated; hosting status confirmed.
evidence.shows: The moderation mode is a factual claim the marketing must match.

transition_in.introduces: Public cases that show the cost of getting the mode wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Human review exists for three reasons, the grey zone, labels and the law, and each calls for a different queue design.

evidence.what: A suspected fake rental with ten contacts in its first hour outranks a possibly miscategorized sofa.
evidence.shows: Grey-zone queues are ordered by expected harm times uncertainty.

transition_in.introduces: Where human judgement sits in the pipeline.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A review queue that almost always ends in the same outcome should become an automated rule, and a rule reviewers would often overturn should go back to the queue.

evidence.what: Stripe Radar documentation (n.d.).
evidence.shows: A payments rule that transfers to moderation.

transition_in.introduces: When work moves between queues and rules.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The random sample gives the only trust-and-safety number that does not depend on what the detectors already catch.

evidence.what: Integrity Institute for Ofcom (July 2026): review randomly sampled ad impressions and most-viewed ads to estimate prevalence.
evidence.shows: An external recommendation for sampling, which classifieds translate into stratified blind samples of listings and messages.

transition_in.introduces: A queue fed by random sampling.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: LLMs entered production moderation between 2024 and 2026, and the thin public classifieds evidence shows real-time chat image checks and policy taxonomies supplied as prompts.

evidence.what: OLX Group January 2026 post on generative-AI image blocking in chats.
evidence.shows: LLM-era moderation is in production at a classifieds group.

evidence.what: Llama Guard, Inan et al., December 2023.
evidence.shows: A policy taxonomy can be given to a model as a prompt rather than retrained.

transition_in.introduces: The newest detector type.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: My rule for LLMs in a moderation pipeline has four parts: grey zone only, policy agility as the main value, deterministic floors stay, and drafts rather than decisions where the law needs a human.

evidence.what: Tradeyard's 2.3 million new listings a week; DSA complaints must not be decided solely by automated means.
evidence.shows: Cost and law set where LLMs fit.

transition_in.introduces: Where the author would place them.

sections.heading: Enforcement Actions and Their Propagation
sections.controlling_idea: An enforcement action is a rung on a ladder that includes demotion, and it is done only when every consumer that holds a copy has applied and acknowledged it.

advances_thesis.how: Argues the propagation half of the thesis.

flow.rationale: First the range of actions, including demotion, then where any action must take effect, the event that makes it happen, and the failure when it does not, ending on the Veldmark incident.

transition_in.carries_over: The pipeline, in which the decision service decides.
transition_in.introduces: The actions it takes and how they reach every system.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Removal is one rung of a ladder of actions the decision service chooses from, and often not the right one.

evidence.what: Integrity Institute for Ofcom (2026): graduated ladder from nudge to suspension; payment freezes need a higher evidentiary threshold.
evidence.shows: External backing for a graduated ladder.

evidence.what: Eight-rung ladder: action, target, trigger, whether a statement of reasons is needed.
evidence.shows: Most rungs restrict a user and need a statement of reasons.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because Article 17 of the DSA covers demotion, a ranking system that quietly pushes suspected scams down is taking a moderation decision, so trust-based down-ranking belongs behind the decision service.

evidence.what: Transparency Database value DECISION_VISIBILITY_CONTENT_DEMOTED.
evidence.shows: The regulator's own schema treats demotion as a decision.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A removal is not finished when the listing's status changes, because search, alerts, recommendations, messaging, SEO pages, ads, payments, partner feeds, profile badges and analytics each hold their own copy.

transition_in.introduces: The event pattern that makes them obey and proves it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Without propagation, enforcement causes Ghost Inventory, and a fraudulent listing in a digest after removal sends buyers to a scammer under the platform's brand, so enforcement should ride the unpublish mechanism with higher priority.

sections.heading: Intake, Cases and Appeals
sections.controlling_idea: Notices, cases, appeals and statements of reasons are entities linked to decision records, so redress and regulatory output follow from the record instead of being built as separate projects.

advances_thesis.how: Argues that review and redress hang off the decision record.

flow.rationale: Follows a complaint from arrival as a notice, to a case, to a decision that can be appealed, to the statement of reasons that reports it.

transition_in.introduces: The other ways violations arrive.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Detection is only one way violations arrive: users, rights holders, authorities, banks and trusted flaggers send notices too.
Because Article 16 of the DSA sets what a notice must contain and what the platform must do with it, a notice is an entity with a lifecycle, not an e-mail in a support inbox.

evidence.what: DSA Art. 16 (notice contents, confirmation, timely decision, outcome, disclosure of automation) and Art. 22 (trusted flaggers).
evidence.shows: The law defines the fields and steps.

evidence.what: Notice fields and why the architecture needs each.
evidence.shows: Turns the legal duties into a data model.

transition_in.introduces: What the law requires of a notice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Case management wins or loses reviewers' productivity through ordinary features: grouping, evidence views, cross-brand history where lawful, reason templates, timers and quality sampling.

evidence.what: Figure 5: case lifecycle with Decided and Enforced as separate states and appeals as new decisions.
evidence.shows: A decision is not in effect until it has propagated.

transition_in.introduces: The case they become.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Article 20 of the DSA requires a free electronic complaint system for at least six months after a decision, decided under qualified staff and not solely by automated means.

evidence.what: DSA Arts. 20 and 21.
evidence.shows: Sets the legal frame for appeals.

transition_in.introduces: How users contest them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three rules follow: an appeal creates a new decision linked to the original, evidence must outlive the complaint window, and reversals are the best labels the platform gets.

transition_in.introduces: The architectural rules they imply.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every restriction needs a statement of reasons to the user and a copy without personal data in the DSA Transparency Database, which shows the scale involved.

evidence.what: About 4.4 billion statements from 375 platforms in the 180 days to 19 October 2026; 41% fully automated.
evidence.shows: The volume is far beyond hand-written notices.

transition_in.introduces: The notice every restricting decision produces.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At Tradeyard NL's volume statements of reasons can only be generated from a decision record, so the record is the upstream design and the regulatory output is a view of it.

evidence.what: About 1.9% of about 1.05 million new Dutch listings a week removed: about 20,000 statements a week from listing removals alone; Veldmark had five exporters.
evidence.shows: Hand-writing or per-brand exporters do not scale.

transition_in.introduces: Tradeyard NL's own volume.

sections.heading: Measuring Trust and Safety
sections.controlling_idea: The platform is judged on harm, speed and accuracy measured from samples and decision records, not on activity, and Veldmark's sample shows how far activity numbers can mislead.

advances_thesis.how: Argues the measurement claim with definitions and Veldmark's numbers.

flow.rationale: The claim and the metric definitions come first, then the practices that make them trustworthy, then Veldmark's numbers as evidence and the reasoning behind its targets. With Veldmark's 0.6% first, the reader would meet prevalence before it is defined.

transition_in.carries_over: The decision record as the source of regulatory output.
transition_in.introduces: Metrics as its other output, and how they are usually built wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Activity numbers say how busy the team is, not whether the marketplace is safe, so the platform needs metrics of harm, speed and accuracy, each with its own way of misleading.

evidence.what: A model that misses a new scam reduces removals and queue sizes at once.
evidence.shows: Activity metrics can improve while harm grows.

evidence.what: Prevalence, exposure-weighted prevalence, time to action, precision, recall, overturn rate, report rate, reviewer agreement: definition, what it tells, how it misleads.
evidence.shows: Defines each metric and its trap.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The numbers are trustworthy only when computed from decision records and samples rather than operational logs, and reported per policy and per detector.

evidence.what: 'Precision 96%' hiding a phishing rule at 99.5% and a counterfeit rule at 70%.
evidence.shows: Shows why aggregates mislead.

transition_in.introduces: Two practices that make them trustworthy.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's first blind sample found about three times the prevalence that removal counts suggested, mostly in harms the detectors could not see.

evidence.what: April 2027: 4,000 Tradeyard NL listings a week, 20 strata; about 0.6% violating against 0.2% assumed; phone-repair services and contact details in images.
evidence.shows: The sample measures what detectors miss.

evidence.what: Figure 6: dashboard 0.2% against sample 0.6%.
evidence.shows: Activity versus harm.

transition_in.introduces: Veldmark's first measurement.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Tradeyard's weekly queue numbers set the shared platform's design targets for end of 2028.

evidence.what: 2.3M to about 2.4M listings; 94% to 96% automated; about 138,000 to about 96,000 reviews; 158 moderators, all on review queues, to about 135 (about 120 on review queues, 96,000 at about 800 each, and about 15 on sampling and appeals); median time to action on fraud reports 3 h 10 min to under 30 min; overturn rate measured per policy with an alert above 10%.
evidence.shows: Turns the metrics into targets.

transition_in.introduces: The targets set from it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The design moved moderators to sampling and appeals rather than removing them, and expected the automation gain from three sources.

evidence.what: About 15 moderators moved; sources: queues turned into rules, an OCR detector for contact details in images, actor-level decisions on rings.
evidence.shows: Explains how the targets were to be reached.

transition_in.introduces: What the targets meant for people and where the gain comes from.

sections.heading: One Platform for Four Brands: What to Share
sections.controlling_idea: A group shares the trust-and-safety machinery and evidence, shares signals only where its Data Protection Officer approves them, and keeps policy content, thresholds, reviewers and vertical detectors with each brand.

transition_in.carries_over: The parts of the platform and their numbers, built since Ingrid's question.
transition_in.introduces: The answer to her question: what the group shares and what stays with each brand.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's rule of sharing platforms, not products, splits trust and safety into machinery the group shares and policy judgement each brand keeps as a tenant of the shared platform.

evidence.what: Twelve components with share, share where lawful, share the registry, or local, and the reasoning.
evidence.shows: Applies the principle component by component.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Sharing signals across brands is a data protection question before it is an engineering one, and Veldmark's architecture enforces the line its Data Protection Officer drew.

evidence.what: Lucía Ortega approved a shared list of hashed phones, e-mails, IBANs and device identifiers of accounts terminated for fraud, with purpose, two-year retention and an impact assessment; not raw content or behavior.
evidence.shows: Shows what can cross brands and how the store design holds the line.

transition_in.introduces: The constraint the table hides.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Keybridge is deliberately not a tenant, because a neutral SaaS business inside the group needs an explicit data boundary, which Figure 7's tenancy split shows.

evidence.what: Veldmark's March 2027 commitment not to use Keybridge agency data for Hearthly's advantage.
evidence.shows: Explains why decisions on Keybridge-originated listings stay Hearthly's.

evidence.what: Figure 7: tenancy split, machinery shared, overlays and detectors per tenant, Keybridge not a tenant.
evidence.shows: The split drawn as tenants.

transition_in.carries_over: The tenancy split and the line on what may cross brands.
transition_in.introduces: The one Veldmark business kept outside the split altogether.

sections.heading: Vertical Differences
sections.controlling_idea: Harms, control points and detectors differ by vertical, so a group platform must accept vertical detectors and policies as tenant content.

advances_thesis.how: Shows why some parts stay local.

transition_in.carries_over: The local side of Figure 7's tenancy split: policy overlays, vertical detectors and thresholds.
transition_in.introduces: How brands differ where their verticals differ.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The vertical table explains why vertical detectors and policies must be first-class tenant content: Hearthly's key detector is stolen-photo matching and Motorvane's key control is dealer verification.

evidence.what: General, real estate, automotive and jobs: harms, supply mix, control point, pre-moderation tolerance, vertical policy, typical detector.
evidence.shows: Each vertical has its own harms and controls.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.controlling_idea: Each choice of where to build trust and safety and where to put human judgement has a cost, and the group keeps its records and sets time budgets per risk tier.

advances_thesis.how: Compares the alternatives to the chosen design.

transition_in.carries_over: Veldmark's chosen split, shared machinery with local policy and vertical content.
transition_in.introduces: The alternatives it was chosen over, and where human judgement goes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A vendor can supply review capacity but not the records the platform learns from, so the decision record, policy registry and labels stay in-house.

evidence.what: Per-brand stacks, shared platform with local policy, fully central, vendor platform: strengths, weaknesses, right when.
evidence.shows: Shows when each option fits.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Moderation costs liquidity, so the answer is risk tiers with explicit time budgets per tier, reviewed with the general managers who carry the liquidity targets.

evidence.what: More pre-moderation, more automation, LLMs in the grey zone, more sampling: benefit and cost.
evidence.shows: Every place for human judgement has a price.

evidence.what: liquidity-and-network-effects: a listing's first hours matter most.
evidence.shows: Waiting time is lost liquidity.

transition_in.carries_over: Where to build trust and safety.
transition_in.introduces: Where to put human judgement.

sections.heading: Failure Modes
sections.controlling_idea: Ten recurring failure modes show how trust and safety goes wrong when the chapter's separations are missing.

advances_thesis.how: Turns each claim into a failure to watch for.

transition_in.carries_over: How to choose well among the alternatives.
transition_in.introduces: How trust and safety goes wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ten failure modes, from moderation only at creation to badges that outlive an account's integrity (introduced with the actor view and the consumer table), each break one part of the design.

sections.heading: The Chief Architect's View
sections.controlling_idea: Sharing pays from the first year but centralizing judgement destroys value, so the Chief Architect assigns each decision an owner, watches long-term trends and reports harm to the board.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the design into decisions, owners and a board metric.

transition_in.introduces: Who decides what at group level.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Trust and safety is one of the few capabilities where sharing pays from the first year and centralizing too much destroys value, so each decision needs a named owner and an indicator.

evidence.what: Seven decisions with who decides and what to watch.
evidence.shows: Assigns owners and indicators.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three long-term trends belong on the roadmap: trust and safety consumes every event, regulation adds outputs, and adversaries learn the platform.

evidence.what: Veldmark's event backbone (July 2027) came before the shared T&S platform (November 2027).
evidence.shows: Shows the dependency on the event backbone.

transition_in.introduces: The trends to plan for.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The board metric is sampled prevalence of fraudulent listings by brand with its trend, next to time to action on fraud reports.

transition_in.introduces: The one pair of numbers for the board.

sections.heading: Questions to Ask
sections.controlling_idea: Ten review questions test a trust-and-safety design against the chapter's claims.

advances_thesis.how: Turns each claim into a question for a design review.

transition_in.introduces: Questions that check them in a review.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ten questions check a trust-and-safety design, from which component writes decisions to whether labels survive a change of review vendor.

conclusion.heading: From Platform to Adversary
conclusion.synthesis: The question the chapter opened with, what did we remove, why, and did it disappear, is answered by one record: the decision record says what and why under which policy version, the acknowledgements say where it took effect, the sample says how much harm remains, and sharing that record and its machinery is what lets a signal from one brand protect another while policy stays local.
conclusion.so_what: A group that builds the record and the propagation path can answer a regulator, a wrongly blocked seller and its own board from the same data; a group of queues answers each with a new project.

callback.to: The opening question (what did we remove last month, why, and did it actually disappear) and the 7 March phishing account with its unseen Motorvane twin.
callback.how: Under the shared platform the suspension is one decision record citing a policy version, its rule reaches every Tradeyard country through one runtime, the counterparties are warned, and the terminated account's hashed phone number reaches Motorvane through the shared block list.

takeaway.content: Make the decision record and the single-writer rule a group decision, emit enforcement as acknowledged events, measure sampled prevalence, and share machinery while keeping policy local.

hand_off.carries_over: Trust-and-safety-architecture's platform, which deliberately left detection as a slot that detectors plug into, and its closing point that the most demanding detectors face people who study the platform and adapt within days.
hand_off.introduces: That adversary and the detector built for it: the classifieds threat model, fraud signals, the risk scoring service with actor-level scoring, step-up friction and the Barcelona fake-rental ring.
